title: Caterpillars: Nature's Magicians
summary: Stuff You Should Know playlist episode "Caterpillars: Nature's Magicians," part of the Think Spring playlist. Josh and Chuck discuss caterpillars as the larval stage of moths and butterflies: their eat-and-molt life cycle, five instars, body structure (six true legs, prolegs with crochets, about 4,000 muscles), spiracle breathing, and hemolymph. They cover defenses (frass shooting, silk drop-lines, camouflage, spines/setae), Hawaiian snail-eating caterpillars, gregarious caterpillars and silk trails, and the chrysalis and cocoon. They explain complete metamorphosis (holometabolism), the breakdown into a cell soup with imaginal cells over about two weeks, and the ideal pupation temperature. The episode ends with garden management, gregarious caterpillars as tree and crop pests, Bacillus thuringiensis, dangerous caterpillars such as the assassin caterpillar and puss caterpillar, eastern tent caterpillars and horse reproductive loss syndrome, and a listener mail segment about a crossword constructor.

segments.title: Playlist introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Think Spring playlist and says this first episode is about caterpillars.

segments.title: Show opening
segments.summary: Standard show opening with the iHeart intro.

segments.title: Opening banter and credits to Tracy Wilson
segments.summary: Hosts note that the episode draws on insect articles written by Tracy Wilson, and that butterflies have not had their own episode. They say caterpillars are the larval stage of moths and butterflies and that the transformation is remarkable.

segments.title: Caterpillar life cycle and eating
segments.summary: A caterpillar is the larval stage whose life is mainly eating and molting. Caterpillars can eat many times their body size and grow about a hundred times larger before pupating. They molt five times, with the periods between molts called instars, and molting is triggered by a hormone that dissolves the attachment to the old exoskeleton. Researchers at Georgetown reportedly found that caterpillars trained to avoid a smell retained that memory as butterflies.

segments.title: Caterpillar body, legs and muscles
segments.summary: Caterpillars have six true segmented legs and many prolegs with suction cups and crochets. They have about 4,000 muscles, compared with about 629 in humans. They move by crawling or by inching. Their 12 stemmata sense light and dark but they are essentially blind and color blind. Their spiracles bring in oxygen through the tracheae, and their hemolymph carries hormones rather than oxygen.

segments.title: Caterpillar senses, setae and stinging hairs
segments.summary: The hosts discuss caterpillar setae, the spines and hairs that can irritate skin, and the caterpillars' poor vision. They recall handling caterpillars as kids. The hosts also mention that the name caterpillar may come from an old French term meaning shaggy cat.

segments.title: Hawaiian carnivorous caterpillars and camouflage
segments.summary: Most caterpillars are herbivores, but some Hawaiian species eat snails by tying them to twigs with silk and eating them. The hosts also discuss an Australian species that eats ants, leaf camouflage, and eyespots that look like snakes, and groups of caterpillars that line up to look like a snake.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Scheduled break in the episode.

segments.title: Caterpillar defenses: frass, silk drop-lines and feeding habits
segments.summary: Caterpillars defend themselves in several ways. The silver spotted skipper's caterpillar shoots frass up to five feet to avoid being tracked. Some caterpillars feed on small bits of many leaves to hide their presence. Others spin silk lines and drop off a leaf when a predator comes.

segments.title: Silk use and gregarious caterpillar groups
segments.summary: Gregarious caterpillars build large silk nests and tents and lay silk trails to find food and shelter. Trails can be reused by later generations. Living in groups has trade-offs: shared shelter and food-finding versus competition, and disease spreads more easily.

segments.title: Pupation, chrysalis and cocoon
segments.summary: Caterpillars wander off to find a safe place to pupate. Butterfly caterpillars form a hardened chrysalis from their skin; moths spin cocoons. Silk is used to anchor and suspend the pupa in various ways. Terminology is explained: the pupa is the life stage between larva and adult.

segments.title: Inside the chrysalis: cell soup and reconfiguration
segments.summary: Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar breaks down into a cell soup. Some cells such as leg cells are rearranged, while others become imaginal cells, analogous to stem cells, and rebuild the body into a butterfly over about two weeks. Scientists are not sure why this complete metamorphosis evolved, and the hosts discuss the best explanation they found.

segments.title: Metamorphosis reflections and tangents
segments.summary: The hosts reflect on how unusual complete metamorphosis is, and joke about Josh's own transformation. Josh recalls a quip about Christopher Hitchens.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Scheduled break in the episode.

segments.title: Pupation timing and temperature
segments.summary: Pupation takes about two weeks on average, depending on weather. Some species overwinter in the chrysalis or cocoon. The ideal temperature mentioned is 21 degrees Celsius, about 70 degrees Fahrenheit (the hosts converted it to 84.6 F with an arithmetic error corrected in the transcript flow).

segments.title: Caterpillars in gardens and pest control
segments.summary: Caterpillars in gardens are usually not a major problem, and they pollinate and feed birds. Gregarious caterpillars such as gypsy moths can defoliate forests and crops. Prevention through removing egg rings is recommended. Bacillus thuringiensis is discussed as an organic control that kills all caterpillars it infects.

segments.title: Dangerous caterpillars
segments.summary: The assassin caterpillar (Lonomia obliqua) is discussed as an anticoagulant venom that has reportedly caused several hundred deaths in South America. The puss caterpillar in North America causes painful stings. Eastern tent caterpillars are linked to mare reproductive loss syndrome in horses that eat them.

segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss doing a two-part episode on butterflies.
